newsitem.title: UK: Probe ordered into sleaze in British parliament.
newsitem.headline: Probe ordered into sleaze in British parliament.

text.p: The British parliament's standards watchdog on Monday ordered an emergency probe into allegations of sleaze that could bedevil the ruling Conservatives in the runup to the general election.
Its decision came after House of Commons speaker Betty Boothroyd told lawmakers she was seriously concerned about allegations members had taken cash in return for asking questions in parliament.
"The reputation of the House as a whole has been called into question. As Speaker I am bound to be concerned about that," she told members returning from their summer recess.
In a forthright statement, Boothroyd said she wanted "the very serious allegations" made against a number of members of parliament to be resolved as soon as possible.
The latest case involves allegations that former trade minister Neil Hamilton accepted cash in return for asking parliamentary questions, in breach of House of Commons rules.

Hamilton has denied the charges, but two weeks ago dropped a libel action against the Guardian newspaper which highlighted the story. Hamilton said he could not afford the legal fees and the Guardian responded by printing fresh allegations.

With an election no more than seven months away, Prime Minister John Major is under constant pressure over his handling of the sleaze issue. Rebel Conservative MP Peter Thurnham quit in protest over the weekend to join the Liberal Democrats, and Major has a majority of just two in parliament.
After a three-hour meeting, the Commons Standards and Provileges Committee decided on an emergency investigation into the whole "cash-for-questions" affair.
The committee said it had formally asked the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards, Sir Gordon Downey, to carry out an inquiry "as a matter of urgency".
Boothroyd insisted that the committee's proceedings should be "as transparent as possible" to restore the public's badly dented confidence in parliament.
Britain's main opposition parties, Labour and the Liberal Democrats, had taken the unusual step earlier of joining up to call for more inquiries.

Their parliamentary managers told a news conference they were worried about allegations that Conservative party managers sought to influence a key committee which governs the conduct of members of parliament.
"It is important that the scope of the enquiry should be comprehensive," said Labour chief whip Donald Dewar.
Dewar and the Liberal Democrat whip, Archie Kirkwood, said Downey should have more resources and more powers if needed.

They also said MPs would be requesting an investigation by Boothroyd into whether David Willetts, then a government whip but now a treasury minister, broke parliamentary rules by suggesting a key committee should clear Hamilton.
